senses.gloss: Śilaka Śālāvatya (‘descendant of Śalāvant’) is the name of a teacher, a contemporary of Calkitāyana dālbhya and Pravāhaṇa jaivala, in the Chāndogya upaniṣad (i. 8, 1).
1. Śilpa means ‘art,’ of which three kinds--nṛtya, ‘dance’; gīta, ‘song’; and vādita, ‘instrumental music,’ are enumerated in the kauṣītaki brāhmaṇa (xxix. 5).

2. Śilpa Kaśyapa is named in the last vaṃśa (list of teachers) in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad as a teacher, a pupil of kaśyapa naidhruvi.
Foot notes vi. 4, 33 (Mādhyaṃdina = vi. 5, 3 kāṇva).

Silācī is, in the Atharvaveda, the name of a healing plant, also called lākṣā.
Foot notes v. 5, 1, 8. Cf. Bloomfield, Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 419; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 228.

Silāñjālā, which the commentator reads as Śalāñjālā, is the name of a plant, perhaps a ‘grain creeper,’ in the Atharvaveda. The kauśika sūtra reads the word as Śilāñjālā. Cf. Silāeī.
Foot notes vi. 16, 4.
ii. 16. Cf. Bloomfield, Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 466; Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 292, 293.
Sīla, ‘plough,’ is found in the Kapiṣṭhala Saṃhitā (xxviii. 8).

Sīlamāvatī in the Rigveda is, according to Ludwig, the name of a river; but this is most improbable. Sāyaṇa thinks the word means ‘rich in hemp.’
Foot notes x. 75, 8.
Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 200.
Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 429; Bo7htlingk, Dictionary, s.v.; Geldner, Rigveda, Glossar, 195.
